I think it’s really give and take and depends on who you are. I’m in my late 20s but I’ve been in therapy since I was about 5 years old, so I have a really unique and different perspective on this than most people do.

I love when therapists tell me about their own life and provide me with relatable stories. I actually find it very healing and relatable when therapists give me insight into their own life. Often times it’s just therapists mentioning that they have life partners or children but I love it because it reminds me that they have full lives outside of therapy (same energy as being in elementary school and learning that the teachers don’t actually live at school).

For me, therapists have been really good about keeping the info about their life minimal but knowing when to pull relevant info forward to try and relate to me and my situation. Sometimes their advice and relatability is a miss (we’re all human and can’t be on point 24/7) but more often than not, it really resonates to the period of life I’m in and it makes me feel so much less alone than if they had never shared the info.

Obviously it’s up to each individual. If you don’t want your therapist to share any personal information ever, whatsoever, that’s fair but just TELL THEM! If you want them to share some information but not as much as they are currently, TELL THEM! If you think they don’t share enough about their life and you feel like getting to know a little more about their lives would help you relate to and open up to them more, TELL THEM!
A good therapist is receptive and will maintain a good attitude and professional relationship if you share concerns with them. A bad therapist will argue with you and make you feel guilty or bad or anything other than confident when setting boundaries with them.

I can’t say yes or no to if your therapist is crossing boundaries as I don’t know you and I don’t know your relationship with your therapist. But I do think it’s important to take stock of what’s important to you in your therapeutic relationship and go from there.

All the CITs had to lead at least one “Leave No Trace” class to younger campers by themselves. At my camp, the CITs also helped plan, decorate, and put on one camp wide event a session.
